strengths: Novel and well-motivated data generation framework: the evolutionary skew-product construction with chaoticity selection (0-1 test, power spectrum, Lyapunov estimation) yields a genuinely new, extensible dataset of 2×10^4 chaotic systems, addressing the hard problem of sampling based on dynamical diversity rather than mere parameter jitter.

Strong empirical results: Panda outperforms comparable-scale time series foundation models (Chronos 20M including SFT, TimesFM, TimeMOE) zero-shot across 9.3×10^3 held-out systems, on multiple metrics (sMAPE, MAE, MSE, Spearman), and generalizes to real experimental systems (double pendulum, C. elegans, coupled oscillator networks).

Architecture is well-grounded in dynamical systems theory rather than ad hoc: channel attention justified by channel coupling (validated via the electronic circuit coupling-strength experiment), polynomial/Fourier dynamics embedding grounded in eDMD/Koopman theory, patching justified via Takens' theorem, and the ablations isolate each component.

Emergent PDE forecasting (KS, von Kármán vortex street) from a model trained purely on low-dimensional ODEs is a striking and practically interesting result, supported by quantitative comparisons against baselines.

The diversity scaling law (holding total timepoints constant while varying number of unique systems) is a genuinely novel finding distinct from conventional data-scaling laws, and is well connected to theory (Pesin's theorem, topological information saturation).

Interpretability analyses (attention maps showing recurrence-map structure, frequency-probing revealing nonlinear resonance lattice, spatio-temporal mixing analysis, Grassberger-Procaccia correlation dimension of completions) go well beyond typical forecasting papers and strengthen the claim that the model learns dynamics, not just patterns.
Extensive appendix with qualitative forecast examples, additional metrics, completions analysis, and reproducibility details (training hyperparameters, hardware, integration tolerances).
weaknesses: The held-out test systems are generated by the same skew-product construction (from 20 held-out founders), so the zero-shot evaluation may favor models adapted to this data distribution; generalization to fully independent dynamical families is tested only on a handful of experimental datasets.

Baseline set is somewhat narrow and comparison fairness is unclear: the strongest baseline (Chronos-SFT) was fine-tuned on Panda's own training dataset; no comparison to strong in-domain methods (reservoir computing, specialized neural ODE/SDE models) or to a fine-tuned Panda variant on the experimental datasets to establish the value of zero-shot transfer.
Model scale is small (~20M params) and training details (e.g., only 3 channels sampled during training) raise questions about how results would scale; the paper does not ablate model size.

The MLM pretraining interacts non-trivially with the dynamics embedding (MLM hurts autoregressive rollout performance), which is acknowledged but left unresolved; the practical recommendation requires case-by-case choices.

The scaling law is fit on only eight points with one seed apparently per split; confidence in the functional form (and exponents) is limited, and no multiple-seed variance is reported for the scaling experiments.

Evaluation is dominated by pointwise accuracy metrics; for chaotic systems, long-horizon statistical fidelity (invariant measures, spectra, attractor geometry) is arguably more meaningful and is only partially addressed (correlation dimension for completions only).

Some terminology/claims are loose (e.g., 'emergent,' 'spontaneously develops'), and there are minor writing issues (typos such as 'exclusely', 'vortext', a broken sentence in Section 5.2) that slightly reduce polish.

Missing discussion of failure modes: no characterization of which held-out systems Panda fails on (e.g., by Lyapunov exponent, attractor dimension), which would clarify the boundary of the claimed universality.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated data contribution: an evolutionary/skew-product framework that discovers 2×10^4 new chaotic ODEs with rigorous chaoticity filtering (0-1 test, near-recurrence, power spectrum, Lyapunov estimation), going beyond simple parameter perturbation of known systems.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: 9.3×10^3 held-out systems, multiple metrics (sMAPE, MAE, MSE, Spearman), multiple horizons including autoregressive rollout, and comparison against competitive time-series foundation models (Chronos 20M both zero-shot and fine-tuned, TimesFM 200M, Time-MOE 50M).

Convincing ablations of the dynamics-motivated design choices (channel attention, dynamics embedding, MLM pretraining), including an honest reporting of the complex MLM/embedding interaction rather than overselling.

Interesting emergent findings: zero-shot transfer to experimental systems (double pendulum, C. elegans, oscillator networks) and to PDEs (Kuramoto-Sivashinsky, von Kármán) despite training only on 3-channel ODEs; the scaling study holding token count fixed while varying system diversity is a genuinely distinct contribution from standard data-scaling laws.

Thoughtful interpretability analysis (recurrence-like attention structure, frequency-probing for nonlinear resonance, spatio-temporal mixing analysis in Appendix F) grounded in dynamical systems theory.
weaknesses: Generalization claims are partially overstated: the 9.3×10^3 'held-out' systems are generated by the same skew-product construction and mutation procedures over nearly the same 135-system founder pool (minus 20 held out), so the out-of-domain shift is narrower than the 'unseen dynamical systems' framing suggests; only 3 experimental datasets support the strongest claims.

Missing important baselines from the MLDS literature: no comparison with local/in-domain models (e.g., reservoir computing, next-generation reservoir computing) that represent the state of the art in chaos forecasting, nor a fine-tuned Panda upper bound; the PDE result is only compared to time-series foundation models, not dedicated operator-learning or PDE baselines.

The 'spontaneous PDE forecasting' claim would benefit from controlled analysis (e.g., what happens with channel-only vs. temporal-only components on PDEs, sensitivity to discretization/resolution), as 2 PDE systems is thin evidence.
Scaling-law study spans only 8 points over ~2 orders of magnitude in N_sys with a single seed per point; no error bars over training runs, and the fitted power law (R²=0.9896) may not be robust.

Several interpretability claims (nonlinear resonance, bispectra analogy) are qualitative and somewhat speculative; the causal link between attention structure and forecasting ability is not established.

Training fixes 3 channels via random channel sampling but inference uses arbitrary channel counts; the multivariate generalization mechanism deserves more analysis, and the multivariate setting makes the fixed-horizon (non-autoregressive) design choice's tradeoffs underexplored.

Some writing/consistency issues (e.g., inconsistent notation for skew-product construction, 'VKVS'/'vortext' typos) and the abstract's strong 'universal representation' language exceeds what the evidence strictly supports.

strengths: Novel and substantial dataset contribution: an evolutionary search framework that discovers 2x10^4 new chaotic ODEs via mutation and skew-product recombination of a curated founder pool, with a principled multi-stage chaoticity selection pipeline (0-1 test, recurrence, power spectrum, Lyapunov estimation). This addresses a real gap in sampling dynamical diversity rather than just parameter jitter.

The architecture is well-motivated by dynamical systems theory rather than ad hoc: channel attention grounded in strong channel coupling, patching connected to Takens' embedding, and polynomial/Fourier features grounded in Koopman/eDMD and next-generation reservoir computing. The implicit spatio-temporal coupling analysis in Appendix F.2 is a nice technical touch.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: comparison against multiple modern time series foundation models (Chronos, Chronos-SFT, Time-MoE, TimesFM) across 9.3x10^3 held-out systems, multiple horizons, multiple metrics, plus three real-world experimental datasets (double pendulum, C. elegans, coupled oscillator circuits) with a coupling-strength analysis that directly supports the channel-attention claim.

The diversity-vs-volume scaling study (holding total timepoints fixed while varying number of unique systems vs. initial conditions) is a genuinely interesting and distinct contribution from standard neural scaling laws, and is well connected to classical theory (Pesin's theorem, topological information saturation).

The zero-shot PDE forecasting result (Kuramoto-Sivashinsky, von Karman vortex street) from a model trained only on low-dimensional ODEs is a surprising and compelling emergent capability, and honest reporting of where baselines fail (sMAPE saturation, NaN cases) increases credibility.

Interpretability analysis (recurrence-map-like attention structure, nonlinear resonance lattices vs. a univariate control) goes beyond performance claims and probes mechanism, with an appropriate control experiment.
Honest limitations discussion, including the counterintuitive finding that MLM pretraining hurts autoregressive rollout.
weaknesses: Evaluation distribution concern: held-out test systems are generated by the same skew-product machinery and the same 135-system founder pool as training data (minus 20 held-out founders). 'Zero-shot' generalization within this synthetic generator family may overstate true out-of-distribution capability; the real-world evidence rests on only three experimental datasets.

Missing comparisons to dynamics-specific forecasting baselines: the paper cites Zhang & Gilpin [40] on zero-shot forecasting of chaotic systems and reservoir computing approaches [4, 58], but does not benchmark against these or other MLDS-specialized methods, limiting the strength of the 'competitive zero-shot forecasts' claim.

The scaling-law analysis spans only about two orders of magnitude in N_sys (156 to 2x10^4) with a single functional form fit; calling this a 'neural scaling law' may be stronger than the evidence, and the mechanism is only argued qualitatively.

Some ablation findings are internally messy (dynamics embedding helps without MLM but hurts with it; MLM helps in-domain but hurts rollout), and the final model choice is justified somewhat post hoc around long-horizon rollouts.

Minor but present polish issues: typos ('exclusely', 'vortext street', 'Botton rows', 'soley'), and key quantitative results (e.g., MSE/MAE/Spearman) relegated to the appendix with only sMAPE in the main text.

Emergence claims ('spontaneously develops the ability to predict PDEs') are evocative but the PDE evaluation covers only two benchmark systems in the weakly turbulent regime; broader PDE evaluation (e.g., against PDE foundation models like Poseidon) would substantiate the claim more strongly.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated dataset contribution: an evolutionary search over skew-product couplings with a suite of principled chaos-selection tests (0-1 test, recurrence, power spectrum, Rosenstein Lyapunov estimator, stationarity tests) produces a large (~2x10^4 systems) and diverse pretraining corpus, with evidence (correlation dimension distributions) that it avoids a founder effect.

Strong empirical evaluation: zero-shot forecasting across 9.3x10^3 held-out systems compared against multiple strong foundation model baselines (Chronos 20M/200M with and without SFT, TimesFM 200M, TimeMOE), with Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, median/IQR reporting, and multiple horizons.

Evaluation goes beyond pointwise accuracy to include distributional/invariant metrics (KL divergence, spectral Hellinger distance, correlation dimension, Lyapunov exponent agreement), which is the right way to evaluate chaotic forecasts.

Compelling emergent capability: zero-shot forecasting of PDEs (Kuramoto-Sivashinsky, von Karman vortex street) despite training only on low-dimensional ODEs, and convincing generalization to real experimental data (double pendulum, C. elegans, coupled oscillator circuits).

Interesting and distinct scaling analysis showing that zero-shot error scales with the number of unique dynamical systems (at fixed total timepoints), connected to dynamical systems theory (Pesin's theorem, attractor information content).

Thorough ablations of architecture choices (channel attention, dynamics embedding via polynomial/Fourier features, MLM pretraining, patch length), with honest reporting of trade-offs (e.g., MLM improving completions but degrading autoregressive rollout).
Extensive appendix with qualitative failure-mode analysis, attention map analysis, hyperparameters, hardware details, and many additional result tables supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: The held-out test systems are generated by the same skew-product recombination process as the training data (only 20 of 129 founders are excluded). While descendants of held-out founders are removed, the distributional gap between train and test is limited; the 'zero-shot on unseen systems' claim would be strengthened by evaluating on systems from genuinely different generative processes (e.g., function-library-sampled or LM-generated systems from related work).

Baseline coverage is narrow: comparisons are dominated by time series foundation models (Chronos family, TimesFM, TimeMOE). Missing are dynamics-specific pretrained baselines (e.g., Ziegler et al. 2024 synthetic-data foundation models, latent ODE-based approaches) and standard MLDS forecasters, which would better isolate the contribution.

Some ablation conclusions are murky: the interaction between MLM pretraining and the dynamics embedding is complex and partially contradictory (helps without MLM, hurts with; helps rollout without MLM, hurts with), and the final recommendation relies on a single combination without a fully satisfying explanation.

Baseline fairness concerns: Chronos-SFT baselines were trained with 10x more gradient updates but much smaller batch size, and NaN issues for some baselines (TimeMOE, Spearman correlations) complicate direct comparisons.
Experimental-data evaluation is limited to three datasets, and the PDE evaluation covers only two systems with modest detail on the setup (e.g., only first 64 PCA modes for VKVS).

The scaling law is fit over a limited range (156 to 2x10^4 systems) with a single architecture; the exponent and its generality across model sizes are not explored, and no theory is offered beyond a qualitative connection to Pesin's theorem.
The code availability footnote is blank in the submitted version, which hinders reproducibility assessment.

The 'climate' (attractor preservation) advantage over Chronos-SFT is modest in some metrics (e.g., +9.5% Hellinger at L=128), and regression to the mean on long rollouts is itself a notable limitation that is acknowledged but not resolved.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely open and important question in SciML: out-of-domain generalization for forecasting of dynamical systems, as opposed to the standard in-domain (same-system) forecasting setting.

The evolutionary dataset-generation pipeline (mutation + skew-product recombination + multi-stage chaoticity filtering via the 0-1 test, Rosenstein Lyapunov estimation, stationarity tests) is a thoughtful and novel contribution; the resulting corpus of ~2x10^4 systems with verified invariant properties (correlation dimension preserved, positive Lyapunov exponents, stiffness characterization) is a reusable community resource.

The architecture is well-motivated by dynamical systems theory (Takens embedding for patching, eDMD-style polynomial/Fourier lifted embeddings, channel attention justified by chaotic channel coupling), and the ablations (Fig. 3, 13) directly test each claimed inductive bias rather than merely asserting them.

Evaluation is unusually thorough for this area: 9.3x10^3 held-out systems, multiple short-term (MSE/MAE/sMAPE/Spearman) and long-term distributional metrics (KL divergence of attractor measures, spectral Hellinger distance, Lyapunov exponent recovery), Wilcoxon significance tests with Holm-Sidak correction, medians with IQRs, patch-size ablations, model/dataset scaling, and qualitative failure-mode analysis.

Zero-shot transfer to experimental data (double pendulum, C. elegans, coupled electronic oscillators) and to two weakly-turbulent PDEs (KS, von Karman) is a striking result, and the finding that channel attention advantage grows with inter-channel coupling strength provides a mechanistically interpretable validation of the design choice.

The 'scaling law' with number of unique dynamical systems at fixed total timepoints is an interesting and conceptually distinct contribution relative to standard data-scaling laws, and is connected to theory (Pesin's theorem / topological vs. measure information).
weaknesses: The held-out 'unseen systems' are still generated by the same skew-product recombination process over nearly the same founder pool (only 20 of 129 founders excluded). Zero-shot generalization is therefore largely within the authors' own synthetic distribution; generalization to genuinely out-of-distribution families of dynamics is not convincingly demonstrated.

Baselines are limited to general-purpose time series foundation models (Chronos, TimesFM, TimeMOE). There is no comparison against dynamics-specific pretrained or local models (e.g., reservoir computing, the authors' cited related work such as Ziegler et al. 2024 or Seifner et al. 2025), so it is unclear whether Panda's advantage stems from the proposed inductive biases or simply from training on chaotic ODE trajectories.

Some quantitative gains are modest: the spectral Hellinger improvement over Chronos-SFT is ~10%, and the fitted scaling exponent is small (N_sys^-0.155). The KL divergence means carry very large standard deviations, and the KL is estimated from finite trajectories, raising concerns about estimator reliability.

The 'emergent PDE forecasting' claim is based on only two PDE benchmarks, one of which is PCA-reduced before inference; this narrow evaluation does not strongly support the broad 'emergent' framing in the abstract and contributions.

Reproducibility is incomplete in the submitted draft: the code-availability footnote and several footnotes (4, 5, 6) are empty, which is unacceptable for a paper whose central contribution includes a dataset and pretrained model.

Some design choices are under-justified: fixing inputs to 3 channels during training (sampling channels at random) is ad hoc, and the interaction between MLM pretraining and the dynamics embedding is reported as inconsistent (helps without MLM, hurts with MLM), leaving the final configuration choice somewhat empirical and its generalization uncertain.

The paper claims baselines were trained/fine-tuned fairly (equalized timepoints), but Chronos-SFT received 10x more gradient updates than Panda due to batch-size constraints; this asymmetry is acknowledged but not fully resolved, and the direction of bias on the comparison is unclear.

strengths: Novel and substantial contribution: an evolutionary-search framework that discovers ~2×10^4 novel chaotic ODEs via mutation, skew-product recombination, and a principled suite of attractor tests (0-1 chaos test, recurrence, spectral, Rosenstein Lyapunov, KPSS/ADF), addressing a real gap in training data for dynamical-systems foundation models.

The architecture is well-motivated by dynamical systems theory rather than borrowed wholesale: patched tokens connected to Takens embedding, kernelized (polynomial/Fourier) patch embeddings tied to Koopman/eDMD and next-generation reservoir computing, and channel attention justified by strong channel coupling.

Comprehensive and unusually rigorous evaluation: zero-shot comparison against multiple time series foundation models (Chronos, Chronos-SFT, TimesFM, TimeMOE) across 9.3×10^3 held-out systems with Wilcoxon significance tests, distributional/attractor metrics (KL divergence, spectral Hellinger distance, correlation dimension), and both deterministic and probabilistic baseline modes.

Demonstrates generalization beyond the training distribution: zero-shot forecasting of real experimental systems (double pendulum, C. elegans posture, coupled oscillators) and emergent zero-shot PDE forecasting (Kuramoto-Sivashinsky, von Kármán vortex street) despite training only on low-dimensional ODEs.

A genuinely distinct scaling-law analysis that holds total timepoints fixed while varying the number of unique systems vs. initial conditions, with a clear theoretical interpretation via Pesin's theorem and topological information content; the coupling-strength analysis on the circuit dataset (Fig. 4) directly supports the channel-attention design claim.

Extensive ablations (channel attention, MLM pretraining, dynamics embedding components, patch length), model scaling experiments up to 72M parameters, failure-mode analysis, and detailed reproducibility information (training details, hardware, integrator settings).
weaknesses: Baselines are restricted to general time series foundation models; there is no comparison to dynamics-specific zero-shot or few-shot forecasting methods (e.g., Zhang & Gilpin 2025, reservoir computing, other SciML pretrained models), which makes it harder to gauge how much of the gain comes from dynamics-specific design versus simply training on in-distribution chaotic data.

The held-out test set is generated by the same skew-product construction and founding pool methodology as the training data (only 20 ancestor systems are held out), so distribution shift between train and test may be narrower than the 'zero-shot on unseen chaotic systems' framing suggests.

Some claims outrun the evidence: the 'neural scaling law for differential equations' is fit over a limited range of ~1.5 decades with a single power-law form; the emergent PDE capability is demonstrated on only two PDEs; and 'emergent' language around the PDE results is somewhat marketing-heavy given the model's fixed 3-channel training and PCA/IC-based preprocessing of the PDE inputs.

Ablation results are not fully coherent: the dynamics embedding helps without MLM but hurts with MLM, and MLM hurts autoregressive rollout; the paper acknowledges but does not resolve this interaction, leaving the architecture's optimal composition somewhat empirical.

The code availability footnote is empty in the manuscript, and some minor issues (typos such as 'sytems', 'vortext street', statistical correlations described as 'statistically correlations', dangling footnote markers) suggest the manuscript needed one more polish pass.

Training restricts inputs to 3 randomly sampled channels while inference uses the full multivariate trajectory; this train/inference mismatch is clever but under-analyzed, and its role in the multivariate generalization results deserves a dedicated ablation.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly framed research question: out-of-domain (zero-shot) generalization for dynamical systems forecasting, distinct from standard in-domain propagator learning.

Significant and novel data contribution: an evolutionary framework (mutation, skew-product recombination, chaoticity/selection filtering) that discovers ~2x10^4 novel chaotic ODEs from a 129-system founder pool, with careful validation (0-1 chaos test, Rosenstein Lyapunov estimator, KPSS/ADF stationarity tests, correlation-dimension and KL analyses showing no founder-effect collapse).

Principled, dynamics-informed architecture: patching justified via Takens embedding, channel attention motivated by chaotic coupling, polynomial/Random-Fourier dynamics embeddings tied to eDMD/Koopman and next-generation reservoir computing, and MLM pretraining for dynamical continuity.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: 9.3x10^3 held-out systems, multiple metrics (sMAPE, MAE, MSE, Spearman, KL divergence, spectral Hellinger distance, correlation dimension), statistically significant Wilcoxon tests with Holm-Sidak correction, and strong baselines including Chronos (zero-shot and SFT), TimesFM, TimeMOE, and DynaMix.

Interesting and well-supported scientific findings: (1) a scaling law in zero-shot error vs. number of unique dynamical systems at fixed total timepoints, connected to Pesin's theorem/topological information; (2) emergent zero-shot PDE forecasting (KS, von Karman) despite ODE-only training; (3) interpretable attention structure (resonance maps, recurrence-like attention patterns); (4) experimental validation on real data (double pendulum, C. elegans, coupled oscillators) showing the channel-attention advantage grows with coupling strength.

Unusual honesty for this area: the paper reports its own failure modes (mean regression at long horizons), shows per-system difference tables where DynaMix/Chronos-SFT beat Panda at long horizons under an alternative KL implementation, and provides an extensive appendix with scaled-up models, patch-size ablations, and reproducibility details.
weaknesses: Scope of 'zero-shot' generalization is somewhat narrower than headline claims: held-out systems are all skew-product descendants of the same 129-system founder pool (with 20 systems held out), so the OOD test distribution is structurally related to training data; generalization to arbitrary symbolic forms outside this family is not directly assessed.

Long-horizon distributional results are mixed: under the geometric-misalignment KL implementation (Table 15) and the mean-regression cutoff analysis (Table 17), baselines outperform Panda, which tempers the claimed long-horizon advantage; the paper's framing relies on choosing the GMM-based KL for the main table.

The comparison to DynaMix is acknowledged by the authors to be unfair (different context lengths, training regime, dimensionality), so the strongest contemporary zero-shot dynamics baseline is only loosely benchmarked.

The scaling-law result (Fig. 5) fits a power law with R^2=0.9896 across only eight dataset splits and holds total timepoints fixed but not other factors (e.g., regularization effects of diverse systems); the reported exponent and its generality deserve more scrutiny.

Emergent PDE forecasting is demonstrated on only two PDEs with a 512-dimensional PCA reduction (VKVS); broader PDE evaluation would strengthen this headline claim, and the FNO/DeepONet baselines are admittedly not directly comparable.

Some ablation results are inconclusive or interactive (dynamics embedding helps without MLM but hurts with it; MLM hurts rollout), leaving the pretraining-objective question partially open; the paper acknowledges this but the main-model design rationale is accordingly muddied.

Training only on 3-channel trajectories (with random channel sampling) versus variable-dimension inference raises questions about channel-order/identity sensitivity and how the model scales to genuinely high-dimensional systems; inference cost on large channel counts is not reported.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely question in scientific machine learning: whether a pretrained 'global' forecast model can generalize to unseen dynamical systems, and the framing (in-domain propagator learning vs. out-of-domain system generalization) is well motivated.

The evolutionary dataset construction pipeline (mutation + skew-product recombination of 129 curated chaotic systems, with a suite of chaoticity/stationarity filters) is a thoughtful and scalable data-generation process, and the appendix provides unusually thorough validation of dataset properties (Lyapunov time distributions, correlation dimension preservation, KL-divergence analysis of lineage diversity, stiffness scores).

Evaluation is extensive: ~9.3k held-out systems, multiple metrics (sMAPE, MAE, MSE, Spearman, KL divergence, spectral Hellinger distance, Lyapunov exponents, correlation dimension), statistical significance testing (Wilcoxon with Holm-Šidák correction), multiple horizons, inference-time comparisons, and scaling experiments (model size and data diversity).

The scaling-law experiment in Section 5.3, holding total timepoints fixed while varying the number of unique systems vs. initial conditions, is a genuinely interesting and well-controlled analysis that connects to classical dynamical systems theory (Pesin's theorem).

The architecture is clearly specified, and the ablations of channel attention, dynamics embeddings, and MLM pretraining are informative, including honest reporting of the complex/contradictory interactions (e.g., MLM hurting rollout performance, dynamics embedding hurting performance when combined with MLM).
weaknesses: The central 'out-of-domain generalization' claim is overstated. Both training and test systems are generated by the same skew-product construction from the same 129-founder population; the test set merely holds out founder lineages. This is lineage-level exclusion within a single generative family, not distribution shift in any meaningful sense. The claim that Panda 'zero-shot forecasts unseen chaotic systems' therefore rests on a much narrower notion of 'unseen' than the paper implies, and the title/abstract framing ('emergent properties', 'zero-shot forecasting of unseen chaotic systems') is stronger than the evidence.

The dataset's effective diversity is questionable: every system is either a parameter perturbation or a driver-response skew product of one of 129 known systems. The paper's own Table 3 shows substantial KL divergence within lineages, and the UMAP analysis is qualitative. It is unclear how much of the apparent generalization is attributable to learning the (fairly regular) skew-product coupling structure rather than 'dynamics' in general.

The emergent PDE forecasting claim (Section 5.4) rests on only two PDEs (KS and von Kármán), with operator-learning baselines that the authors themselves concede are 'not directly comparable' (one-step-ahead, context length 1). Given how prominently this result features in the abstract and contributions, the evidence is thin, and the 512-PCA-mode compression of the vortex street data should be discussed as a potential confound.

Comparison with DynaMix is repeatedly hedged ('a fair comparison is not possible'), yet DynaMix beats Panda on KL divergence and Lyapunov exponent fidelity at long horizons (Tables 15-17, Table 17 shows Panda at 15.25 vs. DynaMix at 3.50 in the mean-regression regime). The main-text claim that Panda 'outperforms the baselines across the board' is not accurate under the alternative KL implementation reported in Appendix F.3, where Panda is worse at every horizon.

The reproducibility statement contains blank URLs ('Python code is available at Weights for the original model are available at...'), and no supplementary repository is verifiable from the submission. For a paper whose contribution centers on a new dataset and checkpoints, this is a significant gap.

Several design choices are justified post hoc rather than principled: the dynamics embedding's benefit disappears under MLM pretraining and the conclusion is essentially 'PolyEmbed works best for rollout', which reads as empirical tuning rather than theory-guided design; similarly, the p-RoPE percentage (75%) and wavelength (500) are given without justification.

The interpretability analysis (Sections 5.5, G) is largely qualitative: attention map 'resonance structure' and Toeplitz/block patterns are visually suggestive but no quantitative validation ties these structures to forecasting behavior or known dynamical mechanisms.

Real-world experimental evaluation is limited to three datasets, all compared only against Chronos-SFT rather than the full baseline suite, weakening the generality claim of the real-world transfer result.

strengths: Novel and substantial dataset contribution: the evolutionary discovery pipeline (mutation + skew-product recombination + multi-stage chaoticity filtering) produces ~2x10^4 verifiably chaotic ODEs, a much richer pretraining corpus than prior parameter-jitter approaches over small founder pools. The dataset quality control is thorough (0-1 chaos test, recurrence/power-spectrum tests, Rosenstein Lyapunov estimator, KPSS/ADF stationarity, correlation-dimension preservation checks in the appendix).

Comprehensive and rigorous evaluation: comparisons on 9.3x10^3 held-out systems across multiple horizons and metric families (pointwise sMAPE/MAE/MSE/Spearman plus attractor-level KL divergence, spectral Hellinger distance, correlation dimension, maximum Lyapunov exponents), with Wilcoxon significance tests, an inference-efficiency comparison, and probabilistic-mode baselines.

Honest and informative ablations: the analysis of channel attention, dynamics embeddings (polynomial/RFF features motivated by eDMD), and MLM pretraining is unusually candid about complex interactions (e.g., MLM helping short-horizon accuracy but hurting rollout), which strengthens credibility rather than overselling the architecture.

Genuinely interesting findings beyond the main benchmark: the diversity-vs-trajectories scaling law (holding total timepoints fixed) is a novel and theoretically motivated result tied to Pesin's theorem, and the zero-shot transfer to chaotic PDEs (KS, von Karman) and real experimental systems (double pendulum, C. elegans, coupled circuits) is a compelling emergent-capability result.

Good interpretability analysis: attention-rollout entropy resonance maps, recurrence-map-like attention structure, and the univariate ablation control give mechanistic insight and support the channel-coupling claim; the spatio-temporal coupling derivation in Appendix G is a nice theoretical touch.

Extensive appendix material (training details, hyperparameters, failure modes including mean regression, patch-length study, scaled-up 72M checkpoints and scaled-up Chronos baselines) supports reproducibility and depth.
weaknesses: Data distribution concerns limit the strength of the 'zero-shot unseen systems' claim: all train and test systems are skew-product recombinations (plus parameter jitter) of the same 129 founder systems, and the coupling scheme is fixed and additive. The test set is thus structurally inside the training distribution family; generalization to genuinely different system classes (e.g., non-autonomous, discontinuous, delay-differential, or non-skew high-dimensional flows) is untested in the main ODE benchmark.

Comparisons to the closest related work are caveat-heavy: DynaMix is acknowledged as not directly comparable (context length, dimensionality, original experiment setting differ), so the primary evidence rests on transformer TSFM baselines; a like-for-like comparison against the strongest recurrent/MLDS methods would strengthen the contribution.

Some central claims are stated more strongly than the evidence: 'emergent' PDE forecasting and 'neural scaling law' rest on only two PDE benchmarks and eight scaling points, respectively; the KL results depend on a custom GMM estimator whose bias/robustness is not validated (though an alternative implementation is helpfully included and shows reversed sign at long horizons, which the text handles transparently).

Experimental real-world evaluation is narrow: three datasets, with Chronos-SFT as the only zero-shot baseline in Figure 4; no fine-tuned specialized baselines (e.g., local RC or per-system neural models) to quantify the practical gap.

Reproducibility statement is incomplete as submitted: the code and weight URLs in Section 8 are blank placeholders, and footnote 1 code link is missing; given the dataset release is central to the contribution, this needs fixing before camera-ready.

Architecture novelty is moderate: the model is a PatchTST variant with channel-attention interleaving and a feature-augmented patch embedding; each component is individually well-motivated but incremental, and the combined-effect story (dynamics embedding helps without MLM but hurts with it) complicates the architectural narrative.
